sources.title: Maryam Mirzakhani (Q1771279) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-16): English label 'Maryam Mirzakhani', description 'Iranian mathematician (1977-2017)', instance of human, born 1977 (the entity carries three day values, 3, 5 and 12 May), died 2017 (day given as 14 and 15 July), Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

International Mathematical Union, 'The Work of Maryam Mirzakhani' (press release for the Fields Medal 2014, with a biographical note; 4 pages) -- CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the Union's own account calls her contributions to geometry and dynamical systems striking and highly original; explains her counting of simple closed geodesics on hyperbolic surfaces (asymptotically a constant times L to the power 6g-6), the volume calculations in moduli space from which she deduced it, the new and completely unexpected proof of Witten's conjecture, her result that Thurston's earthquake flow is chaotic, and the breakthrough with Alex Eskin and, in part, Amir Mohammadi showing that complex geodesics and their closures in moduli space are surprisingly regular, analogous to Marina Ratner's results on homogeneous spaces; and says she combines superb technical ability, bold ambition, far-reaching vision and deep curiosity. Award-body prose written at the time of the prize by the Union (admiring, expert); read in full.

International Mathematical Union, 'Fields Medallists 2014 awardees with brief citations' and 'Fields Medals 2014 - Awardees and Contributions' (web pages) -- the official citation (the Fields Medal is awarded for her outstanding contributions to the dynamics and geometry of Riemann surfaces and their moduli spaces), a short account of her stunning advances, the earthquake-flow result (ergodic and mixing) and the proof that the closure of a complex geodesic is an algebraic subvariety; the second page also carries the Union's statement that its texts and the prize-winner photographs on that page are copyright free. Award-body text; read the Mirzakhani entries in full.

Erica Klarreich, 'A Tenacious Explorer of Abstract Surfaces', Quanta Magazine (editorially independent publication of the Simons Foundation), 12 August 2014 -- a profile published the day of the Fields Medal ceremony, drawing on interviews with Mirzakhani and with Curtis McMullen (her doctoral adviser), Alex Eskin (collaborator), Benson Farb, Anton Zorich, Alex Wright, her school friend Roya Beheshti and her husband Jan Vondrak: her early schooling and Olympiad medals, her graduate-school questioning, the thesis and its three papers, her description of herself as slow and of mathematics as like writing a novel, her habit of doodling on giant sheets of paper to stay connected to a problem, the billiards collaboration with Eskin and the setbacks along the way, and her disinclination to be the face of anything beyond her research. Independent journalism, built on admiring colleagues and on her own words (self material, never sole support); read in full; the passages on her husband's running anecdote, her daughter and the gender balance of mathematics were not used.

'Maryam Mirzakhani: 1977-2017', Notices of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 65 no. 10, November 2018, pp. 1221-1247, communicated by Helene Barcelo and Stephen Kennedy (reminiscences section; PDF hosted by Celebratio Mathematica) -- tributes by her school friend Roya Beheshti; graduate-school peers Izzet Coskun, Laura DeMarco and David Dumas; Ramin Takloo-Bighash; the Princeton colleagues Elon Lindenstrauss and Peter Sarnak; Yahya Tabesh (Sharif University); her collaborator Alex Eskin (who describes the years-long project on orbit closures); her students Jenya Sapir and Danielle Rasooly; Howard Masur; and the MSRI directors Barcelo and Eisenbud (her service on its scientific advisory committee). Posthumous memorial pieces by friends, colleagues and students, admiring in tone but rich in specific episodes, and including some counter-notes (the media's 'genius' portrait, 'cryptic' conversations, a torn test, a reserved manner). Read in full; the passages on her illness, family, private life, cooking and dancing, social and political views and the Iran-Israel remark were not used.

'Maryam Mirzakhani: 1977-2017', Notices of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 65 no. 10, November 2018 (expository pieces and epilogue): Scott Wolpert, 'Maryam Mirzakhani and Hyperbolic Geometry' (a Teichmuller-theory specialist who studied her thesis manuscripts: her insight to use McShane's identity, results given as broad simple statements); Ursula Hamenstadt, 'Zooming In and Out' (a geometer's account of her new geometric way to study moduli spaces); and Alex Wright and Anton Zorich on dynamics, the Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi 'Magic Wand Theorem' and its use by later papers, with Wright's recollection of working with her at Stanford (a blackboard layered with doodles, hours of discussion, mild suggestions rather than instructions, her advice to know what you want and not get distracted). Expert expositions by specialists who write as readers of her work (Wolpert, Hamenstadt), by her co-author and Stanford colleague (Wright) and by a specialist in the field (Zorich); admiring and posthumous. Read the introductions and the Magic Wand and epilogue sections; the technical mathematics was skimmed; passages on her illness, the birth of her daughter and the Iranian-American group photograph were not used.

Stanford Report, 'Maryam Mirzakhani, Stanford mathematician and Fields Medal winner, dies', 15 July 2017 -- the university's news obituary: first and, to date, only woman to win the Fields Medal since 1936; a self-professed slow mathematician described by colleagues as ambitious, resolute and fearless in the face of problems others would not tackle; her preferred method of doodling on large sheets of white paper; her description of her process as lost in a jungle trying new tricks; Steven Kerckhoff on the originality in how she put disparate pieces together and the novelty of her approach; Ralph Cohen on her teaching and PhD advising. University obituary, institutional and admiring; read in full; the passages on her illness and death, family, the Iranian president's statement and the president of Stanford's tribute were not used.

J. J. O'Connor and E. F. Robertson, 'Maryam Mirzakhani', MacTutor History of Mathematics archive, University of St Andrews (last updated August 2017) -- secondary biography that quotes interviews and prize citations: the 2009 Blumenthal Award citation for her exceptionally creative, highly original thesis; her statement in a Clay Fellowship interview that she is a slow thinker who needs time to clean up her ideas and was glad not to write up her work in a rush; the observation that her next papers appeared three years after the thesis; the Eskin collaboration from 2006. Scholarly popular biography, used to corroborate dates and quotations; read the biography through the honours; its passages on her family, an accident, marriage and her illness were not used.

International Mathematical Union, Committee for Women in Mathematics, gallery page 'Maryam Mirzakhani (1977-2017)' (photograph file Mirzakhani_ICM2014LOC.jpg, 1686 x 1685 pixels, credited 'Photo: Seoul ICM 2014, Courtesy IMU') together with the Union's 'Fields Medals 2014 - Awardees and Contributions' page (which states that its texts and the prize-winner photographs on that page are copyright free) -- checked for the portrait's rights: the gallery page gives only the courtesy credit and the site-wide copyright notice, and the awardee page currently shows no photograph for her. Not used for any scoring; the portrait is held.

Wikimedia Commons category 'Maryam Mirzakhani' and its file pages (for example 'Maryam Mirzakhani in Seoul 2014.jpg', 'Maryam Mirzakhani (cropped).jpg', 'Remise de la medaille Fields a Maryam Mirzakhani.jpg', 'Four Fields medallists plus epsilon.jpg' and the Ettela'at clipping) -- checked through the Commons API and the files' wikitext for licence, source and size: the only clearly licensed single-subject photograph is released at 144 x 200 pixels only; the other candidates are a 145 x 178 crop of a video frame, a group photograph, a 1995 newspaper clipping, a statue and notices. Not used for any scoring; the portrait is held.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_mirza_imu_release, src_mirza_imu_citation, src_mirza_notices_experts, src_mirza_stanford, src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_mactutor | 2003-2014 | award body + expert geometers + university obituary + journalism + biography] The IMU's account calls her contributions striking and highly original, describes the new and completely unexpected proof of Witten's conjecture that came out of her counting of simple closed geodesics, and says her insights integrated methods from algebraic geometry, topology and probability theory; Wolpert, a Teichmuller-theory specialist who studied her thesis manuscripts, calls her use of McShane's identity an especially ingenious and useful insight and notes her results are often simple, broad statements without special hypotheses; Hamenstadt says she developed a new geometric way to study moduli spaces that puts earlier, seemingly unrelated results in harmony; Stanford's obituary quotes Steven Kerckhoff on the originality in how she put disparate pieces together and the novelty of her approach; the 2009 Blumenthal citation (quoted by MacTutor) calls the thesis exceptionally creative and highly original; Farb says in Quanta that solving each of two problems would have been an event and that connecting them was another. The most widely corroborated row, with an award body, independent experts and the press, but almost all of it is retrospective praise, award-body prose or tribute, and it describes results rather than creative acts. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 84 / 0.66 lowered to 82 / 0.62 for award-body prose and retrospective praise (committee texts, a prize citation and obituaries). LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster51, before eligibility): the top rows rest on award-body prose and posthumous tributes with no adversarial source; the slow-pace row leans on her own self-description relayed through profiles, and a deliberate slow pace on deep problems is not the same as low execution speed; claim strength lowered.

intuitive_synthesis.rationale: [src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_imu_release, src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_stanford | 1999-2014 | journalism + award body + student reminiscence + university obituary] McMullen recalls that as a graduate student she would form an imaginary picture in her mind of what must be going on, come to his office, describe it and ask whether it was right, and says she has the ability to generate her own vision; the IMU says she has a strong geometric intuition that lets her grapple directly with the geometry of moduli space and is fluent in a remarkable range of techniques and mathematical cultures; she says she thinks about mathematics in pictures; her student Jenya Sapir remembers that in her lectures she painted landscapes in which the concepts of a talk lived together, and that hints she dropped in conversation proved months later to be the backbone of the best way to understand the problem; Stanford's obituary quotes Kerckhoff on how she put disparate pieces together. The descriptions agree across adviser, award body, student and press, but they report a manner of thinking through other people's recollections, and the one account of her method is partly her own. Strong inference at a moderate confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 78 / 0.58 lowered to 76 / 0.56 for interpretation stronger than behaviour (a thinking style inferred from anecdotes and praise) and self-quotation through shared profiles (the pictures remark).

curiosity.rationale: [src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_notices_experts, src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_imu_release | 1999-2015 | colleague and peer reminiscences + journalism + award body] Coskun, DeMarco and Dumas recall her intense and insightful questioning in graduate school; McMullen (in Quanta) recalls that before his genus-two paper appeared she asked why he had done only genus two, and says that what she sees hints of she wants to understand more clearly; Zorich says she gives the impression of someone excited by all the mathematics around her; Lindenstrauss found her energetic, sharp and interested in everything and remembers her asking prescient questions from the balcony of an MSRI lecture hall in 2015; Wright relays a student's recollection that she found some aspect of any question, even a naive one, fascinating; the IMU lists deep curiosity among her qualities. Many independent witnesses describe concrete questioning over fifteen years, though all except the IMU line are tributes. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 80 / 0.64 lowered to 78 / 0.60 for admiring-source concentration (posthumous tributes and a profile written for the medal). LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster51, before eligibility): the top rows rest on award-body prose and posthumous tributes with no adversarial source; the slow-pace row leans on her own self-description relayed through profiles, and a deliberate slow pace on deep problems is not the same as low execution speed; claim strength lowered.

persistence.rationale: [src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_stanford | 1999-2013 | school friend + graduate peers + collaborator + journalism + obituary] Beheshti recalls that in 1999 she stayed up all night on a take-home exam problem the two had given up on and had solved it by morning; Coskun, DeMarco and Dumas recall her coming in close to tears holding what must have been the twentieth draft of her thesis, then returning to her office to revise again, and describe a rare dogged tenacity to do better; Eskin describes about two years on the orbit-closure problem before the argument was blocked, more than a year stuck, and another two years to work out the details; Quanta reports problems she had thought about for more than a decade and Eskin's remark that after setbacks she never panicked, and she says she does not give up easily; Lindenstrauss calls her modest, sharp and persistent and says that not reaping low-hanging fruit meant results took time; Stanford's obituary says colleagues describe her as resolute. Several concrete episodes from different witnesses across fifteen years, though all are admiring recollections, and the thesis-draft story is, as its authors note, a ritual all McMullen's students went through. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 84 / 0.68 lowered to 82 / 0.64 for admiring-source concentration (tributes) and self-quotation through shared profiles ('I don't give up easily' is read through Quanta). LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster51, before eligibility): the top rows rest on award-body prose and posthumous tributes with no adversarial source; the slow-pace row leans on her own self-description relayed through profiles, and a deliberate slow pace on deep problems is not the same as low execution speed; claim strength lowered.

deep_focus.rationale: [src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_stanford, src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_notices_experts | 2002-2016 | journalism + obituary + peer and student reminiscences + colleague recollection] Quanta reports, through her husband (the computer scientist Jan Vondrak), huge sheets of paper on the floor and hours spent drawing what looked like the same picture, and quotes her saying that doodling helps her stay connected to a difficult problem without writing down all the details; Stanford's obituary calls doodling on large sheets of white paper her preferred method; Sapir remembers meetings in which, when no idea came, both fell silent and Mirzakhani became engrossed in her drawing pad; Wright recalls discussing mathematics for hours at a time at her blackboard and her advice to know what you want and not get distracted; Beheshti says she avoided public attention, which helped her stay focused on research. Consistent descriptions of long, absorbed work on one problem, but the main account of the hours is a spouse's, relayed by a profile, the method partly rests on her own words and no source times a working day. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 76 / 0.60 lowered to 72 / 0.55 for single-source dependence (the drawing practice rests on Quanta and its repetition in Stanford's obituary) and self-quotation through shared profiles.

collaboration.rationale: [src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_imu_release, src_mirza_notices_experts | 2004-2016 | collaborator and colleague reminiscences + journalism + award body + expository article] Eskin says they began collaborating as soon as they met at Princeton, that for a few years neither mentioned the central problem though each sensed the other working on it, that they then joined forces and that working with her was fun; Quanta quotes him that she is very optimistic, which is infectious, and that working with her makes seemingly hopeless problems feel more solvable; the IMU names Eskin and, in part, Mohammadi as co-authors of the breakthrough on complex geodesics; Lindenstrauss recalls choosing an intermediate problem with her and her patient explanations at the blackboards of Fine Hall; Dumas, DeMarco and Coskun recall that she was happy to let Dumas include in his paper an application connected to the counting problems she and her collaborators had explored; the MSRI directors say she served on its scientific advisory committee from 2012 to 2016 and never missed a meeting; Wright says she spoke in mild suggestions rather than instructions. Against this, Coskun, DeMarco and Dumas describe her as often quite reserved in her interactions with others. Many concrete cooperative episodes from several co-workers and the award body's list of co-authors, but most of the testimony is from collaborators writing tributes. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 76 / 0.60 lowered to 74 / 0.58 for admiring-source concentration (collaborator tributes) and single-source dependence (Eskin's account is repeated in Quanta).

ambiguity_tolerance.rationale: [src_mirza_stanford, src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_quanta | 2006-2014 | obituary quoting an interview + collaborator reminiscence + journalism] Stanford's obituary quotes her describing her process as having no particular recipe, like being lost in a jungle and using all the knowledge you can gather to come up with new tricks, with some luck finding a way out; Eskin recalls that the orbit-closure project began with vague dreams and no concrete plan, that after about two years the argument was blocked, and that they kept talking weekly for more than a year without progress; Quanta quotes Eskin that after setbacks she never panicked and quotes her saying that in her area there are many tools and you do not know which one would work, so it is about being optimistic and trying to connect things. Concrete episodes of working without a known route, but the best descriptions are her own words (repeated by two outlets) and one collaborator's, so strong inference at a moderate confidence.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_notices_experts, src_mirza_mactutor | 1999-2015 | journalism + collaborator and friend reminiscences + expert + biography quoting an interview] McMullen says that what she sees hints of she wants to understand more clearly (he recalls her asking why he had treated only genus two); Eskin says her philosophy was never to go after the low-hanging fruit and that their projects grew more ambitious; Lindenstrauss says she was not trying to reap low-hanging fruit and that this took time; in a Clay Fellowship interview quoted by MacTutor she says she is a slow thinker who needs time to clean up her ideas and appreciated not having to write up her work in a rush; Beheshti says her work was driven by pure joy in advanced mathematics rather than a desire for fame or influence; Wolpert calls her intellectually ambitious and always eager to unravel the next piece of the puzzle. A consistent pattern of choosing depth over quick results from several witnesses, but much of it is the same remark relayed by collaborators and her own statement, and motives are attributed by tribute writers. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 78 / 0.58 lowered to 74 / 0.56 for interpretation stronger than behaviour (motives attributed by tribute writers) and self-quotation through shared profiles.

execution_speed.rationale: [src_mirza_quanta, src_mirza_mactutor, src_mirza_notices_remembered, src_mirza_stanford, src_mirza_notices_experts | 2004-2013 | journalism + biography + collaborator reminiscence + obituary + expert] Quanta says she likes to describe herself as slow, gravitating toward deep problems she can chew on for years, and that some problems have occupied her for more than a decade; Stanford's obituary calls her a self-professed slow mathematician; MacTutor records that her next papers after the 2004 thesis appeared three years later and quotes her saying she needs time to clean up her ideas; Eskin's account puts the orbit-closure project at about two years to a blocked step, more than a year stuck and two more years to finish; Wolpert notes that her number of publications is not so large but their breadth and achievements are very special. A consistently slow pace of completion, described by herself and corroborated by one collaborator's timeline and publication dates; dual-edged because the slowness coexists with unusually deep results. Strong inference because 'slow' is partly her own label and no source measures her pace against peers. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster51, before eligibility): the top rows rest on award-body prose and posthumous tributes with no adversarial source; the slow-pace row leans on her own self-description relayed through profiles, and a deliberate slow pace on deep problems is not the same as low execution speed; claim strength lowered.

portrait.reason: No rights-clear portrait of adequate size was found. (1) The best portrait found is the 1686 x 1685 pixel photograph on the International Mathematical Union's Committee for Women in Mathematics gallery page for Mirzakhani (file Mirzakhani_ICM2014LOC.jpg, credited only 'Photo: Seoul ICM 2014, Courtesy IMU'; photographer not named; a clear head-and-shoulders view taken at the August 2014 Congress). The Union's page 'Fields Medals 2014 - Awardees and Contributions' states that the texts describing the winners' work are copyright free and that this also applies to the photos of the prize winners on that page, but the Mirzakhani entry on that page currently shows no photograph, so the statement cannot be tied to this file, and the gallery page that hosts the file carries only the site-wide notice of copyright by the Union. An archived copy of the 2014 awardee page, which might show the photograph, could not be read: the Wayback Machine answered HTTP 429 and was not bypassed. A scratch copy was downloaded and opened outside the repository (scratchpad w51_mirza/cwm_photo.jpg, 342,601 bytes); nothing was saved to public/portraits. (2) Wikimedia Commons: the only single-subject photograph with a clear licence is 'Maryam Mirzakhani in Seoul 2014.jpg' (Gert-Martin Greuel, Oberwolfach Photo Collection, CC BY-SA 2.0 de, permission confirmed), but its description says the licence covers only this 144 x 200 pixel version (higher-resolution versions carry stricter terms and the logo watermark must stay), too small to use without upscaling; 'Maryam Mirzakhani (cropped).jpg' is 145 x 178 and is a frame from a YouTube video of the medal ceremony by Florian Caullery (the full 1366 x 768 frame shows the presentation by the president of South Korea, and the footage's own provenance is not established); the Monsoon0 photograph from the Congress (3264 x 2448, CC BY-SA 4.0, own work) shows her with her face turned down and partly hidden and a small child in front of her, so it is not a usable portrait; the 1995 Ettela'at newspaper clipping (636 x 513, tagged public domain with no basis stated) shows her as a teenager; the remaining files are a statue, notices and collages. Photographs credited 'Courtesy Stanford News Service', 'Thomas Lin/Quanta Magazine' or 'Photo by Jan Vondrak' (Celebratio Mathematica) carry no open licence. Next step: write to the IMU Secretariat (imu.info@mathunion.org) or its Committee for Women in Mathematics (cwm.info@mathunion.org) asking them to confirm that Mirzakhani_ICM2014LOC.jpg is covered by the 'copyright free' statement for the 2014 prize-winner photos and to name the photographer; if confirmed in writing, record the photograph (1686 x 1685, scale down only, never up) with that statement as the licence and sourcePageUrl https://www.mathunion.org/cwm/people/gallery/maryam-mirzakhani.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-16) for Q1771279 returned en label 'Maryam Mirzakhani', description 'Iranian mathematician (1977-2017)', birth 1977 (day values 3, 5 and 12 May; the sources read give 12 May), death 2017 (day 14 and 15 July; the sources read give 14 July), ko label '마리암 미르자카니'; the lead's hint was correct. SLUG/QID CHECK: no existing production or candidate file for slug maryam-mirzakhani or QID Q1771279 in the roster51 worktree (data-pipeline/candidates, src). REGION: west_asia, as for the existing Shirin Ebadi and Omar Khayyam candidates (Iranian origin; she grew up in Tehran and studied at Sharif University before leaving for Harvard). Wikidata also lists United States citizenship, which no source read confirms, so nationalityCodes carries only IR. ERA: contemporary (her career ran 2004-2017; precedent Benazir Bhutto). VOCABULARY: occupation mathematician, field mathematics, impact domains scientific and historical, tags theorist and mentor (her advising is described by Stanford's Ralph Cohen and by two of her students in the Notices memorial), archetypes scholarly_specialist and scientific_explorer are existing ids used by other candidates. PREFLIGHT RESULT: zero-politics, two or more independent perspectives, a substantive non-self behavioural source and a canonical significance source were all obtainable before deep research; a rights-clear portrait was NOT (see PORTRAIT). ZERO POLITICS: no political, military, diplomatic or nationalist material is scored or carded; the sources' political and social remarks (Beheshti's recollection of teenage debates, the Iran-Israel remark in Lindenstrauss's tribute, the Iranian president's statement quoted by Stanford, the gender-balance paragraph in Quanta and her remark about not wanting to be the face of anything, the school principal's stand on a girls' Olympiad team) are unscored and appear in no row, card or moment. DECEASED SUBJECT (2017): only documented public professional behaviour is scored. Excluded entirely, with no inference from them: her illness and treatment, the circumstances and fact of her death, her family (husband, daughter, parents and siblings), her private life and character remarks about it (cooking, dancing, humour, privacy), the 1998 bus accident in MacTutor, and any explanation of her working habits by illness, bereavement or private circumstances; her husband is cited only as a witness to her working practice in Quanta. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: International Mathematical Union, 'The Work of Maryam Mirzakhani' (press release for the Fields Medal 2014; https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/IMU/Prizes/Fields/2014/news_release_mirzakhani.pdf), read in full: striking and highly original contributions to geometry and dynamical systems, the thesis results, the earthquake flow and the Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi theorem; supported by the official citation page, Quanta, the Notices memorial, Stanford's obituary and MacTutor. READ (8 substantive sources plus orientation and portrait checks): the IMU release; the IMU citation and awardee pages; Quanta's profile; the AMS Notices memorial issue (reminiscences by 15 authors, one of which, Vafa's, concerns only her last month and was not used, and the expository pieces by Wolpert, Hamenstadt, and Wright and Zorich); Stanford's obituary; MacTutor. All were downloaded as full text and read directly, not through a summarising tool. PERSPECTIVES: the award body (IMU); independent journalism (Quanta) built on her adviser, collaborators and her own words; geometers who write as readers of her work or as colleagues in her area (Wolpert, Hamenstadt, Kerckhoff); a school friend, graduate-school peers, collaborators (Eskin, Lindenstrauss, Wright), students (Sapir, Rasooly), Princeton and MSRI colleagues; a university obituary (Stanford); and a biography quoting her interviews. NO ADVERSARIAL SOURCE EXISTS among those read (she died young and the material is posthumous or prize-time praise), so counter-evidence is internal and is recorded in the rows: her own remarks that she is slow and that avoiding low-hanging fruit tortures you, a peer's warning that the media's 'genius' portrait is not the person she knew, Sapir's 'cryptic' conversations, Wolpert's note that her exposition moves at a varied pace, and Coskun, DeMarco and Dumas on her reserved manner and the torn test. CALIBRATION: because every source is admiring or retrospective and the behavioural detail comes from a small circle (McMullen, Eskin, Vondrak, Zorich, Wright), no score exceeds 82 and no confidence exceeds 0.64. Nine rows are kept; none is padded. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): seven of the nine rows were lowered once after a re-read of the strongest rows (creative originality 84/0.66 to 82/0.62, intuitive synthesis 78/0.58 to 76/0.56, curiosity 80/0.64 to 78/0.60, persistence 84/0.68 to 82/0.64, deep focus 76/0.60 to 72/0.55, collaboration 76/0.60 to 74/0.58, mastery orientation 78/0.58 to 74/0.56) for award-body prose, retrospective praise, admiring-source concentration, single-source dependence, interpretation stronger than behaviour and self-quotation through shared profiles; ambiguity tolerance (68/0.50) and execution speed (34/0.50) were not changed; each lowered row's rationale ends with its own note. TRAITS NOT SCORED: independent thinking and proactive agency (the sources describe her own vision and a few helpful acts, but these overlap the originality, curiosity and collaboration rows); cross-domain range (her work bridges subfields of mathematics rather than unrelated fields); risk tolerance, decisiveness and conflict tolerance (nothing describes the stakes or her choices); perfectionism and detail orientation (the twentieth thesis draft is a ritual her peers say all of McMullen's students shared); social assertiveness, persuasiveness and leadership drive (she is described as reserved, and her committee and editorial roles show service, not drive); achievement drive and impact motivation (her stated motive is joy in the mathematics, and attributions of wider motives come from tribute writers or from Stanford's president); belief updating, adaptability and resourcefulness (no documented instance); aesthetic sensitivity (she speaks of the beauty of mathematics in one quoted line, which is not behaviour). FACT CONFLICTS RECORDED: (1) the Stanford start date (2008 in the IMU's biography and MacTutor, 2009 in Stanford's obituary), so the cards give no year; (2) birth and death days differ across Wikidata and sources (the sources read agree on 12 May 1977 and 14 July 2017); (3) Quanta says 'a monumental collaboration' and Farb 'probably the theorem of the decade', which is an opinion and is not used as fact; (4) the Magic Wand Theorem is a joint result of Eskin, Mirzakhani and, for the orbit-closure part, Mohammadi, so the card says so. NOT OPENED: the New Yorker obituary quoted in the Notices, other profiles (Nature, the Guardian), Wright's survey of her work (arXiv 1905.01753) and Zorich's note on the Magic Wand Theorem, the Harvard and Stanford memorial videos and McMullen's Fields laudation video, the Simons Foundation and Clay interviews (read only as quoted by MacTutor, Quanta and Stanford), the Stanford Daily obituary (downloaded, not read), the technical sections of the Notices expositions, her papers, and the Princeton and MSRI pages. PORTRAIT: HELD (see portrait.reason for the exact blocker and next step); nothing was saved to public/portraits. LEAD REVIEW (Roster51): 4 row(s) lowered before eligibility (the top rows rest on award-body prose and posthumous tributes with no adversarial source; the slow-pace row leans on her own self-description relayed through profiles, and a deliberate slow pace on deep problems is not the same as low execution speed).
